rv.q: Six is irresistible from start to finish.
This 'Six' is a solid '10' for joy.
“Six,” the first new musical of the 2021-2022 season, spreads exactly the kind of energizing, inspirational illumination this town aches for.
It's not a treatise but a lark and a provocation — and a work of blatantly commercial theater.
The songs here, by Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss, are all whip-smart and catchy.
Long may these witty queens reign over the West End
The queens sing their heads off and the audience loses its mind.
For those looking for pure diversion, with bits of sung history tossed in, “Six” will be an unalloyed pleasure.
More musicals could learn this lesson: skip the feints at naturalism and just get down to the songs.

“Six” is a practical, entertaining, well-executed, self-aware show that knows how to please its audience and delivers a soupçon of Broadway pizzazz and good humor without asking a lot or overstaying its welcome.
As spectacle, it's highly conceived kitsch.
This is definitely a history of the English monarchy for people who found the Dynasty -style salaciousness of The Tudors too highbrow, and your enjoyment may depend on how far puberty is behind you.
Six is a triumph of concept and execution, a historically minded musical that manages to be both educational and genuinely entertaining.
Broadway gets to experience this rockin’ rewrite of 16th-century her-story.
An audience show for a wide audience, Six is a rafter-raising entertainment that’ll get you throwing your proverbial bonnet in the air (but please keep that mask on, for now).

not what you might call a traditional musical, nor what formerly would have been considered a well-crafted one. But it has mass appeal, immediacy, enthusiasm, and an incredibly high sense of style; and it revels in what used to be called “girl power” but can now more properly be described as simply, or not-so-simply, power.

It is one of the cleverest, wittiest, flashiest musicals in town—and sets up home in New York after rave reviews wherever it has played, including the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, where it began life in 2017, and London’s West End.

The songs are, without hyperbole, miracles of modern musical theatre: completely, line-by-line relevant to what is happening onstage while maintaining a universal pop appeal that can play without context.
They have created a generous, funny, provocative show that races by you, grabs your hand and flies up into the stratosphere.
You'll laugh. You'll cry. You'll dance. It's everything a theatre experience should be and more.
Author Hayley Levitt Locations Broadway October 03, 2021. The Broadway company of Six onstage at the Brooks Atkinson Theatre. (© Joan Marcus) I vaguely recall writing one of these reviews already.
SIX was one of the tragedies of the pandemic, set to open on the night Broadway went dark back in March 2020.
But the electricity winds up feeling static.
The major problem with this about-face declaration is that everything said or sung before it doesn’t feel changed, making it come off as either a huge structural misstep or completely insincere.
Are young women finally tired of being pandered to by Broadway musicals?
Notwithstanding the dynamic score, 'Six' is weighed down by a labored book, bargain-basement scenic design, and clunky dance choreography.
There are many features in Six that deserve grades of ten for talent and skill, most especially the sensational cast, each of whom gives a command performance.

Six is as sharp and shiny as a sequinned stiletto heel, and couldn’t have come at a better time… musical variety, bite-sized storytelling and unstoppable performances keep the entertainment level high as the musical subversively builds in emotional depth.
Marlow and Moss skillfully combine pop references with nods to musical genres popular five hundred years ago, making the show the most entertaining history lesson on stage.
The Six strutt forward with queen-like assuredness, demanding to be taken seriously to the sound of whimsical harpsichord remixes and a driving pop score.
I can happily note this smart, silly production remains just as easy to embrace.
Six: The Musical is a fun concept and a fun experience.

cn.t: Critics find SIX an energetic, fun pop concert musical with stellar vocals and infectious girl-power spirit, though some dismiss it as lightweight with a thin book and gimmicky concept that prioritizes spectacle over substance.

lo.t: Entries accepted starting at 9:00 AM the day prior to the performance, cutoff at 6:00 PM the day prior. Winners notified by email and have 60 minutes to claim and pay. Digital tickets emailed one hour prior to performance.
lo.inst: Limit one entry per person, two tickets per winner.

sr.inst: Available on the day of the performance at Lena Horne Theatre box office. Valid Student ID required. Cash or credit card. Limit 2. Minimum of 6 tickets available.

so.inst: Available at the box office on the day of the performance only if the show is sold out. Standing positions at the back of the orchestra. Limit 2.

sg.ra: Lena Horne is one of the smaller Nederlander houses (1,069 seats) and the front orchestra AAA/AA rows sit unusually close to the stage with an unraked front section — TripAdvisor reviewer in Row C reported head-blockage from the flat rake, so row B center is the sweet spot for SIX-style concert staging.

Mezzanine overhang at Lena Horne starts at Row J (Headout/TickPick), so rows E-I stay fully open to the ceiling — critical here because the house has only 18 orchestra rows (AAA-Q) and the overhang drops in early relative to larger Nederlander houses.

Headout and TickPick both pin mezzanine overhang start at Row J — with only 18 orchestra rows total, roughly the back half of the Lena Horne orchestra sits under that overhang and loses upper-stage visibility; NYTix specifically flags the side orchestra seats as 'aren't very comfortable'.

Lena Horne's front mezz is unusually shallow — only 4 rows (A-D) per BroadwayDirect chart — so even Row D sits close to the stage with 'advantageous' sightlines (Headout), and the bar is on the mezzanine level (NYTix) making this the most practical tier in this Nederlander house.

Because the front mezz only has 4 rows at Lena Horne, 'rear' of front mezz (C-D) is still just 3-4 rows from the rail — AVFMS R-D-16 and R-C-26 both reported clear views, and these are priced as value seats while Row A commands premium.

Rear mezz at Lena Horne is 8 rows (E-M) continuous with the front mezz balcony — there's no secondary overhang above it (Broadway-show-tickets.com), and because the house only holds 1,069 seats, AVFMS reviewer in Rear Mezz L row G called it 'excellent vantage without feeling far removed'.

Lena Horne's boxes sit tight to the proscenium of this narrow 1,069-seat Nederlander house, and both NYTix and TickPick explicitly warn the angle is 'extremely skewed' / 'more side-on' — private but not viable for shows with choreography or full-stage staging like SIX.
